idiom_name: hand-written translation module: local structs + conversion functions behind one header, foreign handle kept opaque
implementation_notes: ISO C has neither interfaces nor namespaces, so the layer is a module: one header that exposes only local types (struct acl_order) and conversion functions, and one translation unit that is the single place including the legacy or vendor headers. The foreign connection is held behind an opaque pointer (struct acl_conn * declared in the header, defined only in the .c), the outbound direction is a fallible converter returning a status code (int to_legacy(const struct acl_order *, legacy_order *)), and upstream status codes are mapped into one local error enum. What replaces the classic facade/adapter/translator trio is that module boundary plus the free functions; a struct of function pointers (a hand-built vtable) is worth it only when the layer must be swapped at run time - for tests or for several upstreams.
pitfalls: No namespaces and no access control: every layer symbol needs a prefix (acl_) and every foreign declaration must stay out of the shared header, or the linker and the next includer couple unrelated modules.
Ownership of strings and buffers is manual: copying fields with strncpy/snprintf invites silent truncation and missing NUL terminators, so bounded copies and explicit lengths belong in the converter.
Missing error mapping: forwarding the upstream's errno or status codes to callers re-imports the foreign failure vocabulary the layer exists to hide.
The opaque handle must be opened and closed by the layer; a caller that frees or copies it - or simply forgets acl_close - leaks the upstream connection.
